title: 2027 Workforce Mental Health Trends: How Work Is Changing for Employees
summary: Explore two 2027 workforce mental health predictions: how AI may change employees' sense of purpose and how manager burnout can affect entire teams.
body_markdown:
AI can draft a proposal, summarize a meeting, or answer a question someone once brought to a colleague. That can save time. It can also change whose expertise gets used, how people contribute, and where they find meaning and pride in their work.


These changes are unfolding as managers face[pressures that have been building for years](https://www.modernhealth.com/post/expectations-of-managers-have-grown-support-hasnt-kept-up) . Their jobs now extend far beyond overseeing day-to-day work. They're expected to guide teams through organizational change, support employee well-being, develop talent, and deliver results. Now AI is adding another layer, changing how their teams work and what employees need from them.


Changes in how people work can affect their sense of purpose, their relationships with colleagues, and their ability to perform. Over time, those shifts can influence engagement, collaboration, and employees' desire to stay.


Our upcoming *2027 Workforce Mental Health Trends Report* explores what these developments mean for employees and organizations. We’re starting with two predictions HR and benefits leaders should prepare for now.


‍


## **Prediction 1: AI will raise productivity demands—and put meaningful work at risk**


‍


Concerns about AI in the workplace often center on job security, higher productivity targets, and the pressure to learn new technology. But employees can keep their jobs and still find that the work they value most is changing.


A[study by Microsoft Research and Carnegie Mellon University](https://doi.org/10.1145/3706598.3713778) found that AI-assisted work can shift critical-thinking activities toward checking information, integrating responses, and overseeing tasks.


Consider an employee who once developed ideas, worked through problems, and created something from scratch. Now, AI may produce the first draft, leaving that employee to assess its quality, correct mistakes, and decide what to keep. While those tasks still require skill and judgement, they may offer fewer opportunities to apply personal strengths or feel ownership over the finished result.


There’s also the pressure to accomplish more.


In[Modern Health's survey](https://explore.modernhealth.com/a-new-look-at-how-gl/how-global-employees-use-mental-health-support?utm_campaign=2026-q3-atl&utm_content=report&utm_medium=direct-share&utm_source=sales) of 1,000 U.S. employees, 67% said AI had raised expectations for their productivity. Of that group, 64% reported greater stress as a result.


"As productivity expectations rise, employees can feel pressure to keep doing more, no matter how much they accomplish," says Dr. Jessica Watrous, Chief Clinical Officer at Modern Health. "When that pressure persists, stress can build over time and follow people beyond the workday, making it harder to disconnect and recover."


But workload and stress are only part of the emerging story.


In a recent[Harvard Business Review article](https://hbr.org/2026/11/how-ai-erodes-peoples-sense-of-value-at-work) , researcher Zach Mercurio describes a manager whose coworkers had begun asking AI questions they once brought to him. The change left him questioning how much he mattered.


His experience points to something that employers shouldn’t overlook: Work gives people opportunities to contribute, share expertise, build relationships, and feel needed. As AI changes how people collaborate and what they spend their time doing, some of[those opportunities may disappear](https://www.modernhealth.com/post/workplace-connection-the-evidence-and-trends-employers-should-know) .


This has implications for the business as well as the individual. Employees who feel their knowledge is no longer valued may become less engaged. Teams that turn to AI instead of one another can lose opportunities to problem solve, create, or build trust. Over time, those changes could affect motivation, performance, and employees’ desire to stay.


**Our prediction for 2027:** Rising productivity demands will be only part of AI's impact on workforce mental health. As AI takes on more creative and collaborative work, employees risk losing opportunities to use their strengths, contribute ideas, and feel valued. Employers will need to pay closer attention to what employees gain—and lose—as their roles change.


***Continue reading:***[Managing AI anxiety across your workforce](https://www.modernhealth.com/post/managing-ai-anxiety-across-your-workforce)


### **What employers can do**


Start by looking at how AI changes the experience of work, not just how much time it saves.


Ask employees which parts of their jobs have changed and whether they still have opportunities to use their strengths and contribute ideas. Look at where AI has replaced everyday collaboration and whether teams are losing valuable opportunities to learn from one another.


Employers can also help employees see how their expertise remains essential as roles evolve. Recognize the judgment and creativity behind AI-assisted work, not only the speed of the finished product. Give people opportunities to develop ideas themselves, and consider how time saved through AI could create more room for meaningful work and collaboration.


Productivity expectations need attention, too. Reviewing AI-generated work, correcting errors, and making decisions all take time. Those responsibilities should factor into how employers set goals and measure performance.


[Mental health benefits provide another important form of support](https://www.modernhealth.com/post/managing-ai-anxiety-across-your-workforce) . Coaching can help employees navigate uncertainty, build confidence in changing roles, and strengthen skills for managing stress and communicating their needs. Self-guided resources and clinical care offer additional options when employees need support.


Together, thoughtful AI adoption and accessible mental health care can help employees adapt to change while preserving what makes their contributions valuable.


‍


## **Prediction 2: Manager burnout will increasingly affect entire teams**


‍


A postponed one-on-one may look like a scheduling problem. To an employee struggling with an unclear priority or an unmanageable workload, it can mean another week without guidance.


Multiply those missed conversations across a team, and the effects can grow. Decisions stall. Priorities remain unclear. Problems that might have been resolved early become harder to address. Employees can lose confidence in the support available to them, while the organization risks slower progress, weaker engagement, and declining performance.


[Managers play a central role in preventing those problems](https://www.modernhealth.com/post/managers-as-multipliers-of-organizational-resilience) , but the demands on them have grown considerably.


According to[Gallup's State of the Global Workplace 2026](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/349484/leadership.aspx) , global manager engagement fell from 31% in 2022 to 22% in 2025. Gallup also found that managers' average number of direct reports rose from 10.9 in 2024 to 12.1 in 2025.


At the same time,[managers have taken on greater responsibility](https://www.modernhealth.com/post/expectations-of-managers-have-grown-support-hasnt-kept-up) for employee development, well-being, and organizational change. They're now helping employees navigate AI adoption and shifting roles, often while continuing to carry individual responsibilities of their own.


Research offers insight into how this sustained pressure can affect employees.


A[six-month study of leader–employee pairs](https://doi.org/10.1080/1359432X.2016.1167682) found that leader burnout was associated with subsequent losses in employees' job and personal resources, which were then linked to greater employee burnout.


The findings help explain why manager strain deserves attention beyond the managers experiencing it. When leaders have less capacity to provide guidance, resolve problems, and support their teams, employees can lose resources they rely on to manage their own work and well-being.


"We've spent years talking about how much pressure managers are under. What deserves more attention now is what that pressure means for their employees and the organization as a whole," says Alison Borland, Chief People & Strategy Officer at Modern Health. "When managers are stretched too thin to provide clarity, support, and connection, the effects can spread throughout the entire company."


‍ **Our prediction for 2027:** The effects of long-standing manager strain will become more visible across teams and organizations, with growing implications for employee mental health, engagement, and performance.


### **What employers can do**


Supporting managers starts with understanding what their jobs actually require today.


Look at how manager responsibilities have changed. How much time do managers spend handling competing priorities, individual work, administrative tasks, and organizational change? Do they have enough capacity to coach employees, provide meaningful feedback, and address concerns before they grow?


As teams evolve, employers should also consider whether managers have the training, authority, and resources to meet expectations. Reducing unnecessary demands, clarifying responsibilities, and protecting time for employee development can help managers focus on supporting their teams.


Employee feedback offers another valuable perspective.


Rather than looking only at manager engagement or burnout, employers can assess how employees experience leadership. Do they understand what's expected of them? Can they get timely feedback and guidance? Do they feel comfortable raising concerns? Are workload problems being addressed?


Those insights can reveal where manager strain is already affecting team effectiveness, even[before its consequences appear in broader performance measures](https://www.modernhealth.com/post/the-performance-tax-every-company-pays) .


Mental health benefits are equally important. Managers need support for their own well-being, not only training to help them support others.


Coaching can help managers navigate difficult conversations, strengthen leadership skills, and manage stress during periods of change. Therapy and other clinical care provide support for more complex mental health needs. Employees also benefit from access to a range of care that reflects their individual circumstances.


By giving managers the capacity to lead and access to mental health support, employers can strengthen the day-to-day experience of the people who depend on them.


‍


## **Preparing for the mental health demands of 2027**


‍


AI adoption and manager support often sit in different parts of an organization's strategy. But for employees, both shape the experience of everyday work.


They influence whether people have opportunities to contribute in meaningful ways, feel connected to their colleagues, receive the guidance they need, and have the capacity to do their best work.


Those experiences affect more than individual well-being. They also influence how well teams collaborate, how engaged employees feel, and how effectively organizations adapt to change.


HR and benefits leaders have an important role in these decisions. They can help organizations recognize emerging pressures, understand how changes to work affect employees, and make sure mental health support reflects the full range of workforce needs.


That means bringing employee mental health into conversations about AI adoption, leadership expectations, and organizational performance while ensuring people can access appropriate care as their needs change.
